Adjectives

Describing people & things

★ Why this matters

Adjectives let you describe almost anything · people, places, feelings, objects. This is one of the most immediately useful vocabulary-grammar combinations you'll learn.

ADJECTIVEred
+
NOUNapple

Rule: in English, adjectives go before the noun and never take a plural -s. a red apple → two red apples (not reds).
size · big / smallThey live in a big house with a small garden.
feeling · happyThe children are very happy today.
price · expensive / cheapThis bag is expensive but that one is cheap.
opinion · beautifulThis is a beautiful photo.
difficulty · difficult / easyGrammar can be difficult, but practice makes it easy.
⚠️ Common mistakes
❌I have three reds apples.
tap to see the correct form
✅I have three red apples.
❌She is a woman beautiful.
tap to see the correct form
✅She is a beautiful woman.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Focus on natural sentence rhythm: emphasize the main content words when expressing Adjectives, while keeping grammatical function words unstressed.

More examples

  • He is a tall, friendly man.
  • We ate a delicious dinner.

never~0%

Freq.WordExample
~0%NEVERI never drink coffee at night.
~10%RARELYShe rarely eats fast food.
~30%OCCASIONALLYThey occasionally visit their grandparents.
~50%SOMETIMESI sometimes walk to school.
~70%OFTENJohn often plays football with friends.

Position: adverbs of frequency go before the main verb (I often read) but after the verb to be (She is always late). These percentages are approximate · a rough guide to compare the words, not exact maths.

Focus on natural sentence rhythm: emphasize the main content words when expressing Adverbs of Frequency, while keeping grammatical function words unstressed.

4 All, Both, Either, Neither, None

Part 3 · Describing Things

All, Both, Either, Neither, None

Talking about a whole group, or exactly two things

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can build clear, accurate sentences and communicate confidently in everyday situations.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

👀 What do you notice?

Observe the examples below. Pay attention to word order, endings, and sentence patterns before reading the rule.

Correct · This structure provides explicit grammatical function and clarity.
2. Form check: Does correct usage of All, Both, Either, Neither, None require matching subject, verb, and modifier agreements?
Correct · Accurate form and agreement choices prevent misunderstandings.

Rule: all and none talk about a group (3 or more). Both, either, neither only talk about exactly two things or people.

WordGroup sizeMeaningExample
All3+every one, no exceptionsAll my friends speak English.
Both2 (only)the two togetherBoth books are mine.
Either2 (only)one or the other, your choiceYou can take either bus · they both stop here.
Neither2 (only)not the one, not the otherNeither answer is correct.
None3+not a single one, zeroNone of my friends were late.

💡 Either / neither + singular verb

Either and neither talk about two things, but the verb that follows is singular: Either day is fine. Neither answer is right.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Focus on natural sentence rhythm: emphasize the main content words when expressing All, Both, Either, Neither, None, while keeping grammatical function words unstressed.

5 Articles: A / An / The

Part 1 · Nouns & Pronouns

Articles: A / An / The

Choosing the right article

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can build clear, accurate sentences and communicate confidently in everyday situations.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

👀 What do you notice?

Observe the examples below. Pay attention to word order, endings, and sentence patterns before reading the rule.

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. Function check: What is the primary purpose of using Articles: A / An / The?
Correct · This structure provides explicit grammatical function and clarity.
2. Form check: Does correct usage of Articles: A / An / The require matching subject, verb, and modifier agreements?
Correct · Accurate form and agreement choices prevent misunderstandings.
Is the noun specific and known to both speakers?
YES (Specific)
Use 'THE'
Pass me the salt.
NO (Singular Countable)
Use 'A / AN'
I need an apple.
NO (Plural / Uncountable)
Use 'SOME / Ø'
I want some water.
Example
consonant sound · AI have a dog and a cat.
vowel sound · ANShe has an apple and an egg.
specific thing · THEThe sun is hot. Close the door, please.
general / plural · no articleI like cats. Children love music.

💡 Listen, don't just look

Say the next word. Vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u)? Use an: an apple, an hour. Any other sound? Use a: a dog, a university (starts with a 'y' sound, not a vowel sound).

NEW thinga dog
SAME thing, now knownthe dog

I saw a dog. The dog was brown. · once mentioned, it becomes 'the'.

💭 Think like a native speaker

Articles barely exist in many languages · Russian has none at all. If your language doesn't have them, this repetition (a dog… the dog…) is exactly how English marks 'a new thing' vs 'the thing we both know'.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Focus on natural sentence rhythm: emphasize the main content words when expressing Articles: A / An / The, while keeping grammatical function words unstressed.

⚠️ Common mistakes
❌I have an dog.
tap to see the correct form
✅I have a dog.
❌She is a engineer.
tap to see the correct form
✅She is an engineer.
❌I like the music in general.
tap to see the correct form
✅I like music.

💡 Memory trick

The extra N in an exists just to stop two vowel sounds crashing into each other. Say “a apple” out loud · it's awkward! The n smooths the join: “an apple.”

6 Before & After + -ing

Part 8 · Prepositions & Connectors

Before & After + -ing

Sequencing time and actions clearly

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can sequence your daily activities smoothly by connecting actions with "before + verb-ing" and "after + verb-ing".
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

👀 What do you notice?

Notice the verb form after before and after when there is no subject pronoun:

  • Before leaving the house, I turn off the lights.
  • After eating lunch, we went for a walk.
  • Wash your hands before eating!

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. What form does a verb take immediately following prepositions like 'before' or 'after'?
Correct · Prepositions are followed by -ing verbs (gerunds) or nouns.
2. Can you also use a full clause with a subject (e.g., "after I ate")?
Correct · If a subject is present, use a conjugated verb; if no subject is present, use -ing.
Structure Pattern Formula Example
Preposition + Gerund Before / After + Verb-ING Before going to bed, read a book.
After finishing work, I relax.
Preposition + Noun Before / After + Noun Before class, drink coffee.
After dinner, watch TV.
Preposition + Subject Clause Before / After + Subject + Verb Before I go to bed, I read.
After we finished work, we met up.

Rule Summary:
• Prepositions (before, after, by, without, for) require a noun or an -ing verb.
• Do NOT use base verbs after before/after (❌ before to go / ❌ before go). Always use before going or before I go.

🧠 Think like English

Prepositions in English can never take an infinitive verb (unlike French or Spanish). Whenever a preposition is directly followed by an action, English automatically transforms the action into a noun form using -ing.

⚠️ Common mistakes
❌Before to leave, check your keys.
tap to see the correct form
✅Before leaving, check your keys. (Never use 'to + infinitive' after before/after!)
❌After eat dinner, I go for a walk.
tap to see the correct form
✅After eating dinner, I go for a walk.

💡 Memory Trick

The Preposition -ING Rule:
Preposition + Action = -ING Action!
Before starting, after finishing, without stopping!

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Connects to Prepositions of Time and Conjunctions & Time Connectors.

Correct · Before is followed by the -ing form (leaving).

Correct · After + -ing (finishing).
3. Choose the correct sentence:

9 A0–A1 Confusing Grammar Master Guide

Level A0–A1 Grammar Reference

A0–A1 Confusing Grammar Master Guide

A vs B (vs C) structural contrasts, logic rules, and usage guides for beginner English learners

🎯 Master Goal: Confidently choose the right word, tense, preposition, and question structure without second-guessing yourself in everyday conversation.

👀 What do you notice?

Compare these two sentences: "I work in London." (Permanent job) vs. "I am working in London this week." (Temporary situation). Notice how changing the tense changes the entire meaning!

💡 Check your understanding (CCQs)

Score: 0 / 2
1. Function check: If someone says "I live in Paris", does this mean it is a permanent situation or a temporary 2-day trip?
Correct · Present Simple indicates facts, habits, and permanent situations.
2. Form check: What is the correct question structure for an action verb in Present Simple?
Correct · Action verbs in Present Simple take 'Do' or 'Does' in questions.

🧠 Logic Map: Core A0–A1 Present & Structure Contrasts

Structure AStructure BCore Logic DifferenceKey Examples
Present Simple Present Continuous Habits, routines & facts vs. Happening now or temporary I drink coffee every day. vs. I am drinking coffee now.
Do / Does Is / Are Action verbs vs. Adjectives, nouns, places or -ing continuous Does she work here? vs. Is she at work? / Is she working?
Don't / Doesn't Not / Am not / Isn't Negative for verbs vs. Negative for adjectives/nouns/be I don't know. vs. I am not tired.
No Not No + noun (zero quantity) vs. Not + adjective/verb There is no water. vs. The water is not hot.
In (Time) On (Time) / At (Time) In + long periods (months/years) vs. On + days/dates vs. At + exact time in July, in 2026 | on Monday, on May 5 | at 8:00, at noon
In (Place) On (Place) / At (Place) In = inside container/city vs. On = surface vs. At = specific point/location in the bag, in Paris | on the table | at the door, at the station
Every All Every + singular noun (each member) vs. All + plural noun (group together) Every student has a book. vs. All students have books.
Every day Everyday Two words = adverb (each day) vs. One word = adjective (normal/routine) I study every day. vs. These are my everyday shoes.

🗣️ Pronunciation & Grammar Hint

Remember the golden rule for DOES: After Does or Doesn't, the main verb drops its '-s' and stays simple! Say: "Does she like tea?" (NOT ❌ "Does she likes tea?").

⚠️ Common Beginner Mistake Flips
❌Does she likes coffee?
tap to see the correct form
✅Does she like coffee?
('Does' already carries the 3rd person -s!)
❌I am not like fish.
tap to see the correct form
✅I don't like fish.
(Use 'don't' with action verbs like 'like')
❌I go there every day shoes.
tap to see the correct form
✅These are my everyday shoes. / I go there every day.
('Everyday' = adjective; 'every day' = frequency adverb)

🎯 Can you identify these contrasts?

Permanent job = Present Simple ('works').
2. '___ you tired?'

10 Confusing Verbs, Questions & Negatives

Level A0–A1 Core Confusions

Confusing Verbs, Questions & Negatives

Complete contrast guide for present forms, question auxiliaries, negatives, and verb types

🎯 Communicative Goal: Form accurate present tense sentences, ask natural questions, and express negative preferences without confusing auxiliary verbs.

👀 What do you notice?

Compare these pairs:

  • "Is he a doctor?" (asking about a noun) vs. "Does he work here?" (asking about an action verb)
  • "Are you tired?" (adjective) vs. "Do you like pizza?" (preference verb)
  • "I don't know." (verb negative) vs. "I am not tired." (adjective negative)

🧠 Concept Check Questions (CCQs)

Score: 0 / 3
1. Which verb carries the grammar in 'Does she work here?'
Correct · DO/DOES carries the third-person grammar marker, so the main verb remains base form!
2. Can stative verbs like 'know', 'love', and 'like' usually be used in -ing continuous forms?
Correct · State verbs (know, like, want, need, believe) describe permanent states, not ongoing activities.
3. What is the difference between 'I don't like fish' and 'I hate fish'?
Correct · 'Don't like' is a mild negative preference; 'hate' expresses strong dislike.

1. Present Simple vs Present Continuous (Points 45 & 46)

FeaturePresent SimplePresent Continuous
Core IdeaFacts, routines, habits, repeated actionsHappening around now, temporary situations
StructureSubject + Verb (s/es for he/she/it)am / is / are + Verb-ing
ExamplesI drink coffee every morning. She works at a bank.I am drinking coffee now. She is studying this month.
With ALWAYSNormal habit: He always arrives early.Annoyance or complaint: You are always losing your keys!

2. State Verbs vs Action Verbs (Point 47)

State Verbs: Describe thoughts, feelings, possession, and senses (e.g. know, like, love, want, need, believe, understand, remember, have [possession]). They do NOT normally take continuous -ing forms.

  • ✅ I know the answer. (NOT ❌ I am knowing the answer.)
  • ✅ I have a car. (Possession = state) vs. ✅ I am having lunch. (Action/Activity = continuous)
  • ✅ I think it is good. (Opinion = state) vs. ✅ I am thinking about my future. (Mental activity = continuous)

3. Questions: Do/Does vs Is/Are (Points 48, 49 & 50)

Question FormUsed WithExamples
DO / DOES + subject + verb Action verbs, routines, habits Do you play tennis? Does she live in Paris?
IS / ARE + subject + noun/adj/place/-ing Adjectives, nouns, places, continuous now Are you tired? Is he a doctor? Are you working now?
💡 Logic Trick: If the sentence has an action verb (work, play, live, like), use DO / DOES! If it has an adjective/noun/location, use AM / IS / ARE!

4. Negatives: Don't/Doesn't vs Not vs No (Points 51 & 52)

  • Don't / Doesn't + base verb: Used to negate action verbs. I don't know. She doesn't like coffee.
  • Not (am not / isn't / aren't): Used with adjectives, nouns, and auxiliaries. I am not tired. He is not a doctor.
  • No + Noun: Zero quantity of something. There is no water. I have no money.

Compare: There is no food. (= zero food) vs. The food is not good. (= food exists, but quality is bad).

⚠️ Common Mistake Flips
❌Does she likes tea?
tap to see the correct form
✅Does she like tea?
('Does' carries the grammar, verb stays simple)
❌Is he work in London?
tap to see the correct form
✅Does he work in London? / Is he working in London?
(Action verb habit requires 'Does')
❌I am knowing the answer.
tap to see the correct form
✅I know the answer.
('Know' is a state verb)

🎯 Self-Assessment Checklist

Topic Diagnostic Quiz

Score: 0 / 3
1. '___ she live in Madrid?'
'Live' is an action verb in third person singular → 'Does she live...?'.
2. 'I ___ happy with this answer.'
'Happy' is an adjective → 'I am not happy'.
3. 'You are always ___ your keys!' (expressing annoyance)
Always + Present Continuous expresses annoyance at repeated behavior!

11 Confusing Words & Quantifiers Master Guide

Level A0–A1 Core Confusions

Confusing Words & Quantifiers Master Guide

Complete contrast guide for frequency, quantifiers, adjectives vs adverbs, and similar words

🎯 Communicative Goal: Distinguish similar words and quantifiers accurately, describe degree and frequency, and position adjectives and adverbs correctly.

👀 What do you notice?

Compare these subtle pairs:

  • "I study English every day." (Frequency adverb) vs. "This is my everyday routine." (Adjective)
  • "He is a good driver." (Adjective describing 'driver') vs. "He drives well." (Adverb describing 'drives')
  • "This film is very long." (Acceptable) vs. "This film is too long." (Problem / excessive)

🧠 Concept Check Questions (CCQs)

Score: 0 / 3
1. What is the difference between 'very' and 'too'?
Correct · 'Very' strengthens an adjective (very good); 'too' indicates a negative excess or problem (too expensive).
2. Which word is used for vertical height of people and buildings?
Correct · 'Tall' is used for people and narrow vertical structures; 'high' is used for mountains, walls, and heights above ground.
3. Is 'every day' written as one word or two words when it means 'each day'?
Correct · 'Every day' (two words) = each day; 'everyday' (one word) = common/normal adjective.

1. Quantifiers & Frequency Contrasts (Points 58, 59, 60, 61, 62)

PairRules & DistinctionExamples
EVERY vs ALL Every + singular noun (individual members)
All + plural/uncountable noun (the whole group)		 Every student has a book.
All students passed the exam.
EACH vs EVERY Each = Focus on individuals one by one
Every = Focus on the whole group as individuals		 Each student received a certificate.
Every student must register.
EVERY DAY vs EVERYDAY Every day (two words) = Frequency adverb ("each day")
Everyday (one word) = Adjective ("normal / routine")		 I study English every day.
These are my everyday clothes.
ONCE vs FIRST TIME Once = Frequency ("one time")
First time = Initial experience		 I visit my doctor once a year.
This is my first time in London.
AGO vs BEFORE Ago = Finished past relative to now (with time duration)
Before = Earlier than another moment in past		 I met her two years ago.
I have seen this movie before.

2. Adjective & Adverb Confusions (Points 74, 81, 82, 83, 84, 95)

  • MAYBE vs MAY BE: Maybe = adverb (Maybe he is busy). May be = modal verb phrase (He may be busy).
  • GOOD vs WELL: Good = adjective describing nouns (a good teacher). Well = adverb describing actions (she teaches well).
  • FAST vs QUICKLY: Fast = speed of movement (he runs fast). Quickly = little time required (he finished quickly).
  • HIGH vs TALL: Tall = people and vertical narrow structures (a tall man, a tall building). High = mountains, walls, height above ground (a high mountain, a high wall).
  • BIG vs LARGE vs GREAT: Big = common size word (a big house). Large = formal size / measurement (a large amount). Great = outstanding / important (a great idea).
  • VERY vs TOO: Very = high degree (very good). Too = negative excess / problem (too expensive = cannot buy).

3. Adjective Order & Word Order Rules (Points 123 & 130)

Standard Adjective Order: Opinion ➔ Size ➔ Age ➔ Shape ➔ Colour ➔ Origin ➔ Material ➔ Noun

Example: ✅ a beautiful small old red Italian leather bag (NOT ❌ a leather red small bag).

Adjective & Adverb Position:

  • Adjectives go BEFORE nouns: a big house (NOT ❌ a house big).
  • Adverbs of frequency go BEFORE main verbs, but AFTER the verb to be: I usually drink tea. / I am always tired.
⚠️ Common Confusing Word Flips
❌He drives good.
tap to see the correct form
✅He drives well. / He is a good driver.
('Well' describes the action verb 'drives')
❌Mount Everest is very tall.
tap to see the correct form
✅Mount Everest is very high.
(Mountains take 'high', people and buildings take 'tall')
❌I met him two years before.
tap to see the correct form
✅I met him two years ago.
(Past duration before now requires 'ago')

🎯 Self-Assessment Checklist

Topic Diagnostic Quiz

Score: 0 / 3
1. 'She plays the piano very ___.'
Action verb 'plays' requires the adverb 'well'.
2. 'I moved to Canada three years ___.'
Specific past duration before now = 'ago'.
3. 'My brother is very ___.'
People's height uses 'tall'.

12 Conjunctions

Part 4 · Connecting Words

Conjunctions

And, but, or, because, so, when, if, although

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can link ideas, express reasons, results, conditions, and time, and build clear, fluent English sentences.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.
Situational Context Examples
  • Alex likes coffee and tea.
  • Sarah wanted to go to the park, but it rained.
  • Do you want water or juice?
  • Alex stayed home because he was tired.
  • It was cold, so Sarah wore a coat.
  • Alex listens to music when he walks to work.
  • If it rains tomorrow, we will stay inside.
  • Although it was cold, Alex went for a walk. (receptive recognition)

👀 What do you notice?

Notice how conjunctions connect two words or full ideas (clauses). When if, when, or although starts a sentence, notice the comma , separating the two parts!

🧠 Concept check

  • Does because introduce the cause or reason (Why?) for something? (Yes)
  • Does so introduce the outcome or result (What happened next?)? (Yes)
  • In "If it rains, we stay inside", do we stay inside every day? (No, only on the condition that it rains)
  • Is although used to connect ideas that naturally agree or ideas with a surprising contrast? (Surprising contrast)
FunctionConjunctionExample SentenceUsage Note
AddingANDI have a brother and a sister.Combines similar ideas or items.
ContrastBUTShe is small but strong.Connects opposite or unexpected ideas.
ChoiceORDo you want tea or coffee?Presents options or alternatives.
Reason (Why?)BECAUSEI stayed home because I was ill.Introduces the cause or explanation.
Result (What next?)SOIt was raining, so we stayed home.Introduces the effect or conclusion.
TimeWHENI smile when I see my friends.Points to a specific time or recurring event.
ConditionIFIf you study, you will pass.Introduces a possible situation or requirement.
Surprising ContrastALTHOUGHAlthough he was tired, he worked late.Receptive / Recognition level: Shows unexpected contrast.

🪜 Sentence-Building Ladder

Watch how a short 3-word sentence grows step-by-step into richer communication:

1. Base sentence: I go for a walk.
2. Add info (+ AND): I go for a walk and listen to music.
3. Add contrast (+ BUT): I go for a walk, but it is cold outside.
4. Add reason (+ BECAUSE): I go for a walk because I love fresh air.
5. Add result (+ SO): It is sunny, so I go for a walk.
6. Add condition (+ IF): If the weather is fine, I go for a walk.
7. Add time (+ WHEN): I wear a scarf when I go for a walk.
8. Add surprising contrast (+ ALTHOUGH): Although it is cold, I go for a walk.

🌳 Quick Logic Decision Guide: Which word do I need?

  • ➕ Adding information? ➔ Use AND
  • 🔀 Choosing between options? ➔ Use OR
  • ⚡ Direct contrast? ➔ Use BUT
  • 😲 Surprising contrast? ➔ Recognize ALTHOUGH
  • ❓ Explaining WHY (the cause)? ➔ Use BECAUSE
  • ➡️ Explaining WHAT HAPPENS NEXT (the result)? ➔ Use SO
  • 🔑 Setting a condition (only if)? ➔ Use IF
  • ⏰ Pointing to a time or moment? ➔ Use WHEN

🧠 Think like English: Sentence Connectors

English conjunctions act as bridges between ideas. Word order inside each connected clause stays completely normal: [Subject + Verb] + Conjunction + [Subject + Verb].

When sentence-linking words like If, When, or Although come at the beginning of the sentence, place a comma , after the first clause before continuing to the main thought!

⚠ Common mistakes
❌It was cold, because I put on my jacket.
tap to see the correct form
✅It was cold, so I put on my jacket. (Putting on a jacket is the result, not the cause of cold weather!)
❌Although it was raining, but we went out.
tap to see the correct form
✅Although it was raining, we went out. (Do not double-link with 'although' and 'but' together in one sentence!)
❌I'm tired because I not sleep well.
tap to see the correct form
✅I'm tired because I didn't sleep well.
❌I call you if I will arrive.
tap to see the correct form
✅I will call you when I arrive. / I will call you if I arrive late.

💡 Memory Trick: The Conjunction Compass

BECAUSE = Back to Cause (Look backwards: Why?)
SO = So What Happens Next? (Look forward: Result!)
IF = Key to the Door (Unlocks the result only when condition happens)
WHEN = Clock on the Wall (Marks the exact time of action)

More examples
  • We like pizza and pasta.
  • He is tired, but he is still working.
  • I stayed home because I was ill.
  • She studied hard, so she passed the exam.
  • Call me when you arrive at the station.
  • If you need help, ask the teacher.
  • Although she was late, she didn't miss the bus.

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Combine conjunctions with Present Simple for daily routines, Prepositions of Time for scheduling, or explore Question Words in the A1 English Grammar Manual.

🎯 Can you already use this?

Quick check

Score: 0 / 5
1. 'It was raining, ___ we stayed home.' (result)
So introduces a result.
2. 'I'm happy ___ it's my birthday.' (reason)
Because introduces a reason.
3. 'Do you want tea ___ coffee?'
Or presents a choice between options.
4. '___ it is sunny tomorrow, we will go to the beach.' (condition)
If introduces a condition for a future action.
5. '___ it was cold, Alex didn't wear a heavy jacket.' (surprising contrast)
Although introduces an idea that contrasts unexpectedly with the main clause.

Can you help me? is fine between friends. Could you help me? sounds a little more polite · good for shops, strangers, or your teacher.

Rule: use this/that before a singular noun and these/those before a plural noun. This book / These books.

This vs. it: use this to introduce something new (This is my brother.); once it's known, use it (It's very tall.).

💭 Think like a native speaker

English only marks distance and number here · not gender. French needs ce/cette, but English keeps it to one less thing to track.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

28 English Around the World

Part 5 · Appendix

English Around the World

British, American, Canadian & Australian differences

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can build clear, accurate sentences and communicate confidently in everyday situations.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

👀 What do you notice?

Observe the examples below. Pay attention to word order, endings, and sentence patterns before reading the rule.

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. Function check: What is the primary purpose of using English Around the World?
Correct · This structure provides explicit grammatical function and clarity.
2. Form check: Does correct usage of English Around the World require matching subject, verb, and modifier agreements?
Correct · Accurate form and agreement choices prevent misunderstandings.

★ Why this matters

English differs slightly by country, but everyone understands each other. Here are the differences that matter most for a beginner.

PointWhat changesExample
PossessionUKAU have got · USCA have / have gotI've got a car. = I have a car.
Groups of peopleUKAU singular or plural verb · USCA singular onlyMy team is/are winning.
WeekendUKAU at the weekend · USCA on the weekendSee you at/on the weekend!
OffersUK Shall we…? · USCAAU Should we…?Shall we go? (UK) · Should we go? (US)
Past tense spellingUKAUCA learnt, dreamt · US learned, dreamedI learnt / learned French.
Dates in numbersUKAU day/month/year · US month/day/year5/7/2026 = 5 July (UK) or May 7 (US)

Spelling patterns: colour/color, centre/center, realise/realize, travelling/traveling · the left form is UK/AU/CA, the right is US.

💡 A few everyday words that differ

UK flat / US apartment · UK holiday / US vacation · UK autumn / US fall · UK biscuit / US cookie · UK rubbish / US garbage · UK football / US soccer · UK lift / US elevator

★ Why this matters

Good news: grammar structures elsewhere in this manual work the same way in every variety of English · only these small points change, and native speakers understand all of them.

UK and Australia write dates as day/month/year.

30 Good vs Well & Bad vs Badly

Part 6 · Adverbs & Modifiers

Good vs Well & Bad vs Badly

Adjectives vs Adverbs and Irregular Forms

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can distinguish between describing things/people (Good, Bad) and describing actions/performance (Well, Badly, Fast, Hard) without common beginner mix-ups.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

👀 What do you notice?

Notice how words describe either nouns (things/people) or verbs (actions):

  • She is a good singer. ➔ She sings well.
  • It was a bad game. ➔ They played badly.
  • He is a fast runner. ➔ He runs fast (not fastly!).

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. In the sentence "He speaks English well", what word does "well" modify?
Correct · 'Well' is an adverb that describes the manner of the action 'speaks'.
2. Can you say "He drives fastly"?
Correct · 'Fast', 'hard', and 'late' do not take -ly when functioning as adverbs.
Type Adjective (describes Noun) Adverb (describes Verb) Example Pair
Good / Well Good Well (Irregular!) Good cook ➔ Cooks well
Bad / Badly Bad Badly (-ly regular) Bad driver ➔ Drives badly
Fast / Fast Fast Fast (Irregular, no -ly) Fast car ➔ Drives fast
Hard / Hard Hard Hard (Irregular, no -ly) Hard job ➔ Works hard

Core Rule:
• Use Good / Bad with linking verbs or nouns: She is good. The movie was bad.
• Use Well / Badly with action verbs: She cooks well. He sings badly.
• Note on Health: "I feel well" refers to physical health; "I feel good" refers to emotional mood/state.

🧠 Think like English

Ask yourself: "Am I answering HOW someone does something, or WHAT kind of person/thing they are?"
If HOW ➔ use an adverb (well, badly, quickly, fast).
If WHAT KIND ➔ use an adjective (good, bad, quick, fast).

⚠️ Common mistakes
❌I speak English very good.
tap to see the correct form
✅I speak English very well. (Modifies verb 'speak')
❌He runs very fastly.
tap to see the correct form
✅He runs very fast. ('Fastly' does not exist in English!)
❌She plays the guitar bad.
tap to see the correct form
✅She plays the guitar badly.

💡 Memory Trick

The Action Test:
• Verb Action ➔ WELL (Actions end with Well!)
• Noun Object ➔ GOOD (Good objects!)
A good student learns well!

🔗 Connects to what you already know

Connects to Adverbs of Manner (-ly) and Comparative Adjectives (Better/Worse).

💡 Why Grouping Verbs by Pattern Beats Alphabetical Memory

Organizing irregular verbs into pattern families (such as A-A-A invariant forms, A-B-B past ending shifts, A-B-C vowel series, and phonological rhyme families like sing/sang/sung) activates cognitive schema recognition. 39 The Building Blocks of English

Part 1 · Grammar Knowledge Tree

The Building Blocks of English

Alphabet mechanics, capital letters, spelling, sounds, silent letters, stress, intonation, numbers & time.

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can spell names and contact details, understand common English abbreviations, pronounce word stress, verb/plural endings, and connected speech naturally, write prices and numbers, and communicate dates, times, and fractions accurately.

👀 What do you notice?

Observe the examples below. Pay attention to capital letters, silent letters, word stress patterns, verb endings, and connected speech sounds before reading the rules.

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. Which sentence uses capitalization correctly?
Correct · Capitalize the pronoun “I” and proper names such as London.
2. Which abbreviation means “for example”?
Correct · e.g. comes from Latin exempli gratia and means “for example”. i.e. means “that is”.

Unit 1: The English Alphabet & Mechanics

1.1 Capital Letters vs. Small Letters

Rules: Always capitalize the pronoun I, proper names (David, London), days of the week (Monday), months (May), nationalities (British), and the first word of a sentence.

Example:

My name is John. I live in London and I speak English.

1.2 Alphabetical Order & Dictionary Skills

Ordering words alphabetically relies on comparing letters from left to right: first letter (apple, banana, cat), second letter (cat, coat, cup), or third letter (straight, street, string).

1.3 Spelling Names & Addresses

Dictation phrases for spelling names, emails, and addresses aloud:

How do you spell your name? / Can you spell that, please? / Capital A, double L...

A: How do you spell your last name?
B: S-M-I-T-H.

1.4 Common Abbreviations

Everyday short forms and abbreviations used in written and spoken English:

  • ID: Identity Document
  • TV: Television
  • VIP: Very Important Person
  • e.g.: exempli gratia (for example)
  • i.e.: id est (that is / in other words)
  • PC: Personal Computer
  • UK: United Kingdom
  • US: United States

Unit 2: Sounds & Pronunciation Mechanics

2.1 Vowels vs. Consonants

The English alphabet contains 5 vowel letters (A, E, I, O, U) representing 20 distinct vowel sounds and 21 consonant letters (B, C, D, F, G, H, J, K, L, M, N, P, Q, R, S, T, V, W, X, Y, Z).

2.2 Short vs. Long Vowel Pairs & The Magic-E Rule

Vowel length changes word meaning completely:

  • /ɪ/ vs /iː/ (ship / sheep, sit / seat, fit / feet)
  • /æ/ vs /ɑː/ (cat / car, hat / heart)

The Silent-E / Magic-E Rule: A single silent e at the end of a word turns a short vowel into a long vowel that "says its name":

  • kit /kɪt/ → kite /kaɪt/
  • hop /hɒp/ → hope /həʊp/
  • cut /kʌt/ → cute /kjuːt/

2.3 Common Consonant Digraphs

Two consonant letters written together that make a single new sound:

  • SH /ʃ/: shop, shoe, fish
  • CH /ʧ/: chair, cheese, watch
  • PH /f/: phone, photo, elephant
  • WH /w/ or /h/: white, wheel, who
  • NG /ŋ/: sing, long, English

2.5 Silent Letters in Common Words

Letters that are written but not pronounced:

  • Silent K: know, knee, knife
  • Silent L: listen, talk, walk, half
  • Silent W: write, answer, wrong
  • Silent B: climb, comb

2.6 Word Stress in Nouns & Occupations

In English, most two-syllable nouns and occupations have first-syllable stress:

DOC-tor, TEA-cher, WA-ter, BU-sin-ess

2.7 Sentence Stress & Schwa Sound /ə/

Content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives) are stressed; function words (prepositions, articles, auxiliaries) are unstressed. Unstressed syllables often use the schwa sound /ə/:

about /əˈbaʊt/, doctor /ˈdɒk.tə/, teacher /ˈtiː.tʃə/

2.8 Regular Endings: -ed and -s Pronunciation

Regular past tense -ed has three distinct sounds: /ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/ (wanted, needed), /t/ after unvoiced sounds (worked, stopped), and /d/ after voiced sounds (played, lived).

Plural and 3rd person singular -s / -es endings are pronounced /ɪz/ after sibilants (buses, watches), /s/ after unvoiced sounds (cats, books), and /z/ after voiced sounds (dogs, runs).

2.9 Basic Intonation

  • Rising intonation (↗) in Yes/No questions: Are you ready? ↗
  • Falling intonation (↘) in Wh- questions & statements: Where do you live? ↘ / I live in London. ↘

2.10 Connected Speech & Contractions

In natural speech, words flow together in continuous speech streams. Final consonants link smoothly to initial vowels (an apple ➔ /ənæp.əl/, stand up ➔ /stændʌp/). Unstressed function words reduce to weak schwa forms (fish and chips ➔ /fɪʃ ən ʧɪps/), and contractions combine pronouns and auxiliary verbs seamlessly (it's, I'm, don't, can't).

2.11 R-Controlled Vowels

When a vowel is followed by R, the R controls and alters the vowel sound:

  • AR /ɑː/: car, park, star
  • OR /ɔː/: for, born, short
  • ER, IR, UR /ɜː/: her, bird, turn
  • AIR /eə/ & EAR /ɪə/: fair, near

2.12 Suffix Sound Shifts (-tion, -sion, -cian)

Special suffix endings shift their pronunciation to /ʃən/ or /ʒən/:

  • -tion & -cian /ʃən/: nation /ˈneɪʃən/, musician /mjuːˈzɪʃən/
  • -sion /ʃən/ or /ʒən/: discussion /dɪˈskʌʃən/ (after consonant) vs. vision /ˈvɪʒən/ (after vowel)

Unit 3: Numbers, Money, Dates & Time

3.1 Cardinal Numbers 0–1000 & Stress Rules

Numbers 0–20: zero, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty.

Stress distinction:

  • -teen numbers: stress the second syllable (thir-TEEN, four-TEEN)
  • -ty numbers: stress the first syllable (THIR-ty, FOUR-ty)

Tens & Big Numbers: thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, one hundred, one thousand, one million.

3.2 Ordinal Numbers & Birthdates

Ordinals indicate order or position: 1st (first), 2nd (second), 3rd (third), 4th (fourth), 21st (twenty-first).

Writing dates: The 15th of May 1998 or May 15th, 1998.

3.3 Telephone Numbers, Room Numbers & Email Dictation

Phone numbers: Read digit by digit; 0 is pronounced "oh" or "zero"; repeated numbers use "double" (07700 double nine...).

Email dictation symbols: @ = at, . = dot, - = hyphen/dash, _ = underscore.

3.4 Money, Prices & Currencies

Major currency symbols:

  • $ = Dollar
  • £ = Pound
  • € = Euro

Reading prices aloud:

  • $5.50 = five dollars fifty or five fifty
  • £12.99 = twelve pounds ninety-nine
  • €8.40 = eight euros forty

3.5 Telling the Time

Digital: 7:15 (seven fifteen), 8:30 (eight thirty).

Analog: 7:15 (quarter past seven), 8:30 (half past eight), 8:50 (ten to nine).

3.6 Basic Fractions & Percentages

Fractions: 1/2 = a half, 1/3 = a third, 1/4 = a quarter.

Percentages: 50% = fifty percent, 100% = one hundred percent.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Focus on natural sentence rhythm: emphasize the main content words when expressing The Building Blocks of English, while keeping grammatical function words unstressed.

❌The price is five point fifty pounds.
tap to see the correct form
✅The price is five pounds fifty (£5.50).
❌I have 1/2 of apple.
tap to see the correct form
✅I have a half of an apple / half an apple.

💡 Regular vs. irregular

Regular verbs: add -ed. But common verbs like go, have, see are irregular · they change completely, with no -ed. Learn them one by one.

AffirmativeNegativeQuestion
She worked / She went home.She didn't work / didn't go home.Did she work / go home?

💡 Memory trick

Did is the magic word: once you use it, the main verb always goes back to its plain base form · even irregular ones. Did she go? never Did she went?

Common irregular verbs (go → went, have → had, see → saw…) don't follow the -ed rule at all · see the full grouped list in the Appendix: Irregular Verbs.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Regular '-ed' endings have 3 distinct sounds: /t/ after voiceless consonants (stopped), /d/ after voiced sounds (played), and /ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/ (needed).

STOP is short · one vowel, one final consonant. Picture the last letter looking in a mirror and doubling itself before -ed jumps on: stop → stopped.

53 Play vs Do vs Go

Part 9 · Verbs & Actions

Play vs Do vs Go

Sports, activities, and musical instruments

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can correctly describe your sports, hobbies, physical activities, and musical skills without confusing play, do, and go.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

👀 What do you notice?

Look at the verbs used with different sports and activities:

  • I play football on Saturdays. She plays the piano.
  • He does yoga every morning. We do karate.
  • They go swimming in summer. I go running at 7 AM.

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. Which verb do we use with team sports played with a ball (like football or basketball)?
Correct · 'Play' is used for team sports, ball games, and competitive games.
2. Which verb is used with activities that end in '-ing' (like swimming, running, skiing)?
Correct · 'Go' is used with activities ending in -ing that involve moving from place to place.
Verb Usage Rule Examples
PLAY Team sports, ball games, board games, competitive sports, & musical instruments (with the). play football, play tennis, play chess, play the piano
DO Individual non-team sports, martial arts, exercise routines, and non-ball physical activities. do yoga, do karate, do gymnastics, do exercise
GO Activities ending in -ing that involve movement or traveling outside. go swimming, go running, go skiing, go shopping

Golden Rule: Use Play for ball games and musical instruments (play football, play the guitar).
Use Do for self-contained exercises and martial arts (do yoga, do karate).
Use Go for outdoor/movement activities ending in -ing (go swimming, go running).

🧠 Think like English

English separates hobbies by how you perform them: competitive ball games involve 'playing' against rules or opponents, martial arts and exercises involve 'doing' repetitions, and travelling activities involve 'going' to a venue or moving through space.

tap to see the correct form

tap to see the correct form

❌He plays piano.
tap to see the correct form
✅He plays the piano. (Always include 'the' with musical instruments!)

💡 Memory Trick

P-D-G Formula:
🏀 Play = Points & Pianos (basketball, chess, guitar)
🧘 Do = Discipline & Dojo (yoga, karate)
🏊 Go = Going out with -ING (swimming, running)

RuleSingular &rarr; Plural
Most nouns: + sbook → books, cat → cats

🔊 Pronunciation

Plural -s / -es is pronounced /s/ after unvoiced sounds (cats, books), /z/ after voiced sounds (dogs, days), and /ɪz/ after hissing/buzzing sounds (buses, boxes).

💡 Why -s isn't always enough

Does the word end in -s, -x, -ch or -sh? Add -es: box → boxes. Does it end in consonant + y? Change y to -ies: baby → babies.

Spelling check: say the word out loud. If adding just -s would be hard to say (busess, boxs), that's your sign you need -es instead.

💡 The owner comes first

Find the owner, then add 's right after it: Mike's car. No word for 'of' is needed. Owner already ends in -s (like parents)? Just add the apostrophe: parents' house.

Rule: add 's after a singular owner (the dog's toy) and just ' after a plural noun ending in -s (my parents' house). Use whose to ask about ownership.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Focus on natural sentence rhythm: emphasize the main content words when expressing Whose…? Possessive ’s, while keeping grammatical function words unstressed.

💭 Think like a native speaker

The 's ending is one of the last true 'case endings' left in English · a fossil from a time when English marked grammar with endings the way Russian or German still do today.

57 Preposition Confusions Master Guide

Level A0–A1 Core Confusions

Preposition Confusions Master Guide

Clear A vs B contrast rules for time, location, movement, purpose, and direction

🎯 Communicative Goal: Use the right prepositions for time, place, travel, tools, and movement without confusing similar prepositions.

👀 What do you notice?

Observe how prepositions change meaning:

  • "I went to London." (Destination) vs. "I went to London for work." (Purpose)
  • "I travel by train." (Method of transport) vs. "I cut it with a knife." (Tool/Instrument)
  • "The cat is in the box." (Static position) vs. "The cat jumped into the box." (Movement)

🧠 Concept Check Questions (CCQs)

Score: 0 / 3
1. Do we use 'by' or 'with' for instruments and tools you hold in your hand?
Correct · Use 'with' for physical tools and 'by' for transport methods/agents.
2. What is the difference between 'in front of' and 'before'?
Correct · 'In front of' refers to physical position (in front of the building); 'before' refers to time/order.
3. What preposition follows 'during'?
Correct · 'During' is followed by a noun (during the movie); 'while' is followed by a subject + verb clause.

1. IN vs ON vs AT (Time & Place)

PrepositionTime RulesPlace Rules
IN Long periods (months, years, seasons): in May, in 2026, in summer, in the morning Inside enclosed space, city, country: in the room, in Paris, in France
ON Days and dates: on Monday, on my birthday, on 5 May Touching a surface, floor, street: on the table, on the wall, on the 2nd floor
AT Exact time point: at 5 o'clock, at midnight, at lunchtime Specific location point: at the door, at the station, at work, at school

2. Direction & Origin Contrasts

PairDifference & LogicExamples
TO vs FOR To = Direction / destination
For = Purpose / benefit / duration		 I am going to Paris.
This gift is for you. I studied for 2 hours.
FROM vs OF From = Origin / starting point
Of = Belonging / relationship / part		 I am from Spain.
The capital of France. A cup of tea.
BY vs WITH By = Transport method / agent
With = Physical tool / accompaniment		 I travel by bus. A book by Shakespeare.
I write with a pen. I came with my friend.
ABOUT vs OF About = Topic / subject
Of = Relationship / connection		 We talked about movies.
I know about him. vs. I know him.
INTO vs IN In = Position inside (static)
Into = Movement from outside to inside		 The keys are in the bag.
Put the keys into the bag.
OUT OF vs FROM Out of = Movement inside to outside
From = General origin		 He walked out of the house.
He came from London.

3. Spatial Position & Time Prepositions

  • BETWEEN vs AMONG: Between = two distinct things (between tea and coffee). Among = surrounded by a group (among friends).
  • ABOVE vs OVER: Above = higher level (a picture above the sofa). Over = movement above or covering (the plane flew over the city).
  • UNDER vs BELOW: Under = directly underneath (under the chair). Below = lower level generally (below zero).
  • NEXT TO vs NEAR vs CLOSE TO: Next to = immediately beside. Near / Close to = nearby, short distance away.
  • IN FRONT OF vs BEFORE: In front of = physical position (in front of the shop). Before = time/order (before 5 PM).
  • AFTER vs LATER: After + noun (after work). Later = standalone adverb (See you later).
  • DURING vs WHILE: During + noun (during the lesson). While + clause (while I was studying).
  • UNTIL vs BY: Until = action continues up to a time (wait until 5). By = deadline (finish by Friday).
⚠️ Common Preposition Flips
❌I travel with bus.
tap to see the correct form
✅I travel by bus.
(Transport methods take 'by')
❌I arrived at London.
tap to see the correct form
✅I arrived in London.
(Cities and countries take 'in')
❌She is in front of me in line time.
tap to see the correct form
✅She arrived before me.
(Use 'before' for time order, 'in front of' for physical location)

Movement into an enclosed space requires 'into'.

Deadlines use 'by'. Continuation up to a moment uses 'until'.

Present Continuous

Correct · Present continuous expresses temporary situations around the present time.
SubjectAffirmativeNegativeQuestion
II am workingI am not workingAm I working?
He / She / ItHe is workingHe isn't workingIs he working?
You / We / TheyWe are workingWe aren't workingAre we working?

💡 Two parts, one job each

Two parts: am/is/are (matches the subject) + verb -ing (always the same). Forget the -ing, and it's not 'happening now' anymore.

Spelling of -ing: drop silent -e (make → making); double the last consonant after one vowel (run → running); -ie → y (lie → lying).

∞ Connects to what you already know

The Verb ‘To Be’ · am/is/are here are the same forms, now paired with -ing.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

In natural connected speech, '-ing' ends in the velar nasal /ɪŋ/. The auxiliary 'be' is unstressed and blends into the subject.

More examples

  • She's cooking dinner at the moment.
  • Is it raining?

tap to see the correct form

61 Present Simple

Part 2 · Verbs & Tenses

Present Simple

Routines, habits & facts

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can build clear, accurate sentences and communicate confidently in everyday situations.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

👀 What do you notice?

Observe the examples below. Pay attention to word order, endings, and sentence patterns before reading the rule.

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2

Correct · Present simple describes permanent states, routines, and habits.
2. "I eat breakfast at 8 AM." — Does this mean I am eating breakfast right now?
Correct · Present simple expresses routines, not current in-progress actions.
SubjectAffirmativeNegativeQuestion
I / You / We / TheyI workI don't workDo you work?
He / She / ItShe worksShe doesn't workDoes she work?

💡 Why does the verb change?

Is the subject he, she, it, or a name (like Tom)? Add -s to the verb. Any other subject (I, you, we, they)? No change at all.

💡 Memory trick

He, She, It · one person needs one extra letter: -S. Think of it as the verb wearing a name tag for a single, specific person.

Spelling of he/she/it: most verbs add -s (like → likes); after -ch,-sh,-ss,-x,-o add -es (watch → watches, go → goes); consonant+y → -ies (study → studies); have → has.

💭 Think like a native speaker

That one -s is nearly all that's left of a once-huge verb-ending system · Old English marked every person (I/you/he/we) with a different ending, the way Spanish or Russian verbs still do.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

The third-person '-s' ending varies phonetically: /s/ after voiceless consonants (walks), /z/ after voiced sounds (runs), and /ɪz/ after sibilants (washes).

More examples
  • I get up at seven every day.
  • She works in a school.
  • Do you speak English?

tap to see the correct form

Is there a cat?Yes, there is.No, there isn't.
Are there two cats?Yes, there are.No, there aren't.

💡 Negative + any

In the negative, any often replaces a number: There isn't any milk. (not There isn't some milk).

There vs. it: use there to say something exists; use it for something already mentioned, or weather/time.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Focus on natural sentence rhythm: emphasize the main content words when expressing There is / There are, while keeping grammatical function words unstressed.

More examples

  • Is there a bank near here? · Yes, there is.

71 Too vs Enough

Part 6 · Adverbs & Modifiers

Too vs Enough

Excess (Too) vs Sufficiency (Enough)

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can explain when something is excessive (too hot, too expensive) or sufficient (warm enough, enough money) and place "enough" correctly before nouns and after adjectives.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

👀 What do you notice?

Compare the position and meaning of too and enough:

  • This coffee is too hot to drink. (Excessive / Problem)
  • This tea is warm enough. (Sufficient / Just right)
  • I have enough money for the bus. (Sufficient quantity)

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. Does "too hot" mean it is very hot in a good way, or more than acceptable/desired?
Correct · 'Too' indicates excess that often creates a problem or limitation.
2. Where does 'enough' go when describing an adjective (e.g., tall)?
Correct · Adjectives come BEFORE 'enough' (tall enough, old enough).
Word Position Rule Example
TOO TOO + Adjective / Adverb The room is too cold. He drives too fast.
ENOUGH (Adjective) Adjective + ENOUGH She is old enough to drive. (Not: enough old)
ENOUGH (Noun) ENOUGH + Noun We have enough time. Do you have enough water?

Formulas:
• Too + Adjective = excess (too expensive)
• Adjective + Enough = sufficient degree (big enough)
• Enough + Noun = sufficient quantity (enough chairs)

🧠 Think like English

Don't confuse very with too. Very increases intensity ("This cake is very good!"), while too signals an unwelcome excess or obstacle ("This cake is too sweet for me").

tap to see the correct form
✅I am very happy to meet you! (Use 'very' for positive high degree).
❌We don't have time enough.
tap to see the correct form
✅We don't have enough time. (Enough before nouns!)

💡 Memory Trick

The Sandwich Rule:
• Adjectives come FIRST: Old + Enough
• Nouns come SECOND: Enough + Money
Think: Adjective-Enough-Noun (Enough sits in the middle!)

72 Verb Patterns & Adjective Confusions

Level A0–A1 Core Confusions

Verb Patterns & Adjective Confusions

Mastering infinitives, gerunds, verb + noun structures, and -ed vs -ing adjective feelings

🎯 Communicative Goal: Express desires, needs, hobbies, and emotional states using correct verb complement structures and adjective endings.

👀 What do you notice?

Compare these structures:

  • "I want coffee." (Want + Noun) vs. "I want to drink coffee." (Want + TO + Verb)
  • "The movie is boring." (The movie causes boredom) vs. "I am bored." (I feel bored)
  • "She is good at maths." (Ability) vs. "Exercise is good for you." (Health benefit)

🧠 Concept Check Questions (CCQs)

Score: 0 / 3
1. Does -ed describe a person's feeling or the cause of the feeling?
Correct · People feel -ed (bored, interested); things/situations are -ing (boring, interesting).
2. What follows 'want' when you state an action?
Correct · Want requires 'to + infinitive' for actions: 'I want to go'.
3. What preposition is used for skills and abilities with 'good'?
Correct · Abilities take 'good at'; health/benefits take 'good for'.

1. Like, Love, Hate & Preferences (Points 54, 55, 112)

PatternMeaning / FocusExamples
LIKE + Noun Preference for things / objects I like coffee. She likes books.
LIKE + Verb-ing Enjoyment of the activity itself I like swimming. They love cooking.
LIKE + TO + Verb Habit, choice, or routine choice I like to check my emails in the morning.

2. Want & Need: Noun vs TO + Verb (Points 113 & 114)

  • WANT + Noun: Desiring an object. I want a coffee. He wants a new car.
  • WANT TO + Verb: Desiring an action. I want to drink coffee. He wants to buy a car.
  • NEED + Noun: Requiring an object. I need money. We need help.
  • NEED TO + Verb: Requiring an action. I need to work. We need to leave.

3. Adjectives + TO Verb & Prepositions (Points 119, 120)

  • Adjective + TO + Verb: Expressing feelings or difficulty about an action. I am happy to help. She is ready to leave. It is difficult to understand.
  • GOOD AT vs GOOD FOR:
    • Good AT + noun/ing: Skill or ability. She is good at maths. He is good at playing guitar.
    • Good FOR + noun: Benefit or health. Vegetables are good for you. Running is good for health.

4. Feelings vs Characteristics: -ED vs -ING Adjectives (Points 121, 122)

Adjective EndingFocusExamples
-ED (Feeling) How a person feels inside I am bored. She is interested in history. We are tired.
-ING (Cause) The person, thing, or situation causing the feeling The lesson is boring. History is interesting. Long trips are tiring.

tap to see the correct form
✅I want to buy a car.
('Want' requires 'to + verb')
❌The lesson is very bored.
tap to see the correct form
✅The lesson is very boring. / I am very bored.
('Boring' describes the lesson; 'bored' describes your feeling)
❌She is good in English.
tap to see the correct form
✅She is good at English.
(Abilities require 'good at')

73 Verb Patterns: Infinitive vs -ing

Part 9 · Verb System & Patterns

Verb Patterns: Infinitive vs -ing

Connecting two verbs: Verb + to + Infinitive vs Verb + -ing

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can connect two verbs correctly in English (e.g. want to go, enjoy reading, decide to leave, stop smoking) without guessing prepositions.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

👀 What do you notice?

Look at how the second verb changes depending on the first verb:

  • I want to study English. / She decided to buy a car.
  • We enjoy listening to music. / He stopped smoking.
  • They can swim. / You must wait. (Bare infinitive with modals!)

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. Which pattern follows verbs of future intention or decision (want, decide, hope, need, plan)?
Correct · Verbs pointing to future intentions take 'to + infinitive'.
2. What pattern follows modal verbs like 'can', 'could', 'must', 'should'?
Correct · Modal auxiliaries take the bare infinitive without 'to'.
Pattern Group Trigger Verbs Formula & Example
Verb + TO + Infinitive want, need, decide, hope, plan, learn, agree, promise, try Verb + TO + Base Verb
I want to learn. He decided to leave.
Verb + -ING enjoy, finish, stop, avoid, keep (continue), mind, suggest Verb + Gerund (-ING)
She enjoys reading. They finished eating.
Modal + Bare Infinitive can, could, must, should, may, might Modal + Base Verb (No 'to')
I can drive. You must study.

Master Summary:
• Future / Decisions / Goals: want to, need to, hope to, plan to, decide to.
• Activities / Experience / Habits: enjoy -ing, finish -ing, stop -ing, keep -ing.
• Modals: can, must, should + base verb (NO 'to'!).

🧠 Think like English

In English, 'to' points forward like an arrow toward a goal or decision (decide ➔ to act). On the other hand, -ing looks at the experience of an action as it happens or ends (enjoy ➔ reading).

⚠️ Common mistakes
❌I want go home.
tap to see the correct form
✅I want to go home. (Want requires 'to')
❌She enjoys to play tennis.
tap to see the correct form
✅She enjoys playing tennis. (Enjoy requires -ing!)
❌I can to speak English.
tap to see the correct form
✅I can speak English. (Modals never take 'to')

💡 Memory Trick

The 3-Group Rule:
🎯 Target / Goal ➔ TO + Verb (want to, need to)
🎉 Fun / Experience ➔ -ING (enjoy -ing, finish -ing)
⚡ Modal Superpower ➔ BARE VERB (can run, must go)

74 Who: Subject vs Object Questions

Part 11 · Questions & Negation

Who: Subject vs Object Questions

Who called you? vs Who did you call?

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can ask "Who...?" correctly whether you are asking about the person performing the action (subject) or receiving the action (object).
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

👀 What do you notice?

Compare these two questions with Who:

  • Who called you? (Someone called you. You are asking for the Subject ➔ No auxiliary 'do/did'!)
  • Who did you call? (You called someone. You are asking for the Object ➔ Auxiliary 'did' required!)

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. In "Who broke the window?", is 'Who' the person who performed the breaking (Subject)?
Correct · When Who replaces the Subject, the verb follows directly without do/does/did.
2. In "Who did Sarah meet yesterday?", who performed the meeting?
Correct · Sarah is the subject performing the action, so 'Who' asks for the Object of her meeting.
Question Type Target Structure Formula Example
Subject Question Who performed the action? Who + Main Verb + Object?
(No Do/Does/Did!)		 Who lives in this house?
Who wants ice cream?
Object Question Who received the action? Who + Auxiliary (do/does/did) + Subject + Verb? Who do you live with?
Who did you see at school?

Rule Summary:
• When Who IS the subject ➔ Who + verb directly (Who bought this car?)
• When Who IS NOT the subject ➔ Who + auxiliary + subject + verb (Who did you buy this car from?)

🧠 Think like English

In English, auxiliary verbs (do / does / did) are only needed to flip the subject and verb when the subject is already present in the sentence. If Who itself is the subject, there is nothing to flip!

⚠️ Common mistakes
❌Who did call you last night?
tap to see the correct form
✅Who called you last night? (Subject question: no 'did'!)
❌Who you saw at the party?
tap to see the correct form
✅Who did you see at the party? (Object question: needs 'did'!)

💡 Memory Trick

The Test Answer Shortcut:
• If the answer is "HE / SHE" (Subject) ➔ Question uses No Auxiliary (Who called? ➔ He called!)
• If the answer is "HIM / HER" (Object) ➔ Question uses DO / DID (Who did you call? ➔ I called HIM!)

76 Basic Word Order

Part 1 · Nouns & Pronouns

Basic Word Order

Subject + Verb + Object

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can build clear, correct sentences describing actions, people, and habits in English without confusing your listener.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

👁️ What do you notice?

Look at these two sentences: "She reads books" vs. "Books reads she". Why does only the first one make sense in English? Notice how word position fixes the meaning.

★ Why this matters

Word order is the single most important rule in English. Get this right, and a sentence with mistakes elsewhere is usually still understood; get it wrong, and native speakers may not follow you at all.

Rule: a basic English sentence follows the order Subject → Verb → Object. The subject does the action; the verb is the action; the object receives the action. This order does not usually change.

SUBJECTShe
+
VERBreads
+
OBJECTbooks
1. SUBJECT (Who performs the action?) She / I / They
2. VERB (What action happens?) reads / plays / drives
3. OBJECT (What receives the action?) books / football / a car
Who?She
does what?reads
What?books

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Focus on natural sentence rhythm: emphasize the main content words when expressing Basic Word Order, while keeping grammatical function words unstressed.

More examples
  • I like pizza.
  • They play football.
  • My brother drives a car.
  • The children eat breakfast.

💭 Think like a native speaker

English lost most of its word endings centuries ago, so word order does the job those endings used to do. 'Dog bites man' and 'Man bites dog' use identical words but mean opposite things.

tap to see the correct form
✅I like pizza.

tap to see the correct form
✅She reads books.
❌Football play they.
tap to see the correct form
✅They play football.

1. Obligation check: "You don't have to wear a tie." Does this mean wearing a tie is strictly forbidden or optional?
Correct · 'Don't have to' means something is not necessary (optional), while 'mustn't' means forbidden.
2. Tense check: "I lived in Rome for 2 years." Do I still live in Rome today?
Correct · Past Simple with 'for' indicates a completed finished time period.

🧠 Logic Map: Core A2 Elementary Contrast Systems

Structure AStructure BCore Logic DifferenceKey Examples
Past Simple Present Perfect Finished time (yesterday, in 2020) vs. Unfinished time / Life experience (ever, never, so far) I visited Paris in 2022. vs. I have visited Paris twice.
Will Going to Instant decision or prediction without evidence vs. Prior plan, intention, or clear evidence I'll carry that bag for you! vs. Look at those dark clouds, it's going to rain.
Going to (Future) Present Continuous (Future) Intention/plan vs. Fixed arrangement with time, date, or other person confirmed I am going to study tonight. vs. I am meeting my boss at 3 PM.
Must / Have to Don't have to vs Mustn't Obligation vs. Optional (no necessity) vs. Strictly forbidden rule You must wear a seatbelt. | You don't have to pay. | You mustn't smoke here.
Too Enough Excessive (negative problem, before adj) vs. Sufficient (positive/neutral, after adj) This tea is too hot. vs. He is tall enough to play basketball.
Another Other / Others / The other An + other + singular noun vs. Other + plural noun vs. Pronoun vs. Final remaining option another apple | other books | some like tea, others like coffee | the other shoe
In / On (Place) Into / Onto (Movement) Static position inside/on surface vs. Dynamic directional movement into/onto surface He is in the room. vs. He walked into the room.

🗣️ Pronunciation & Spoken Contrast Note

Notice how modal contractions change spoken force: mustn't drops the 't' sound (/ˈmʌsnt/), while don't have to reduces to /doʊnt hæv tə/ in rapid natural speech.

⚠️ Common Elementary Mistake Flips
❌You mustn't pay for the ticket, it is free.
tap to see the correct form
✅You don't have to pay for the ticket, it is free.
('Don't have to' = optional/unnecessary; 'mustn't' = illegal/forbidden)
❌I have seen him yesterday.
tap to see the correct form
✅I saw him yesterday.
('Yesterday' is a finished time marker, requiring Past Simple)
❌This jacket is enough big for me.
tap to see the correct form
✅This jacket is big enough for me.
('Enough' goes AFTER adjectives)

Correct · Accurate form and agreement choices prevent misunderstandings.
FunctionStructureExample
Past Abilitysubject + could + verbWhen I was five, I could swim.
Polite RequestCould you + verb...?Could you pass the salt, please?
Possibilitysubject + could + verbWe could go to the cinema tonight if you like.

Rule: Could is the past form of can for general abilities (I could swim). In present requests, Could you...? is more polite than Can you...?

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Regular '-ed' endings have 3 distinct sounds: /t/ after voiceless consonants (stopped), /d/ after voiced sounds (played), and /ɪd/ after /t/ or /d/ (needed).

Examples

  • Could you open the window, please?

when / as soon as / before / after / untilUse Present Simple in the time clause (after the conjunction)I will call you when I arrive.

Obligation, prohibition, and lack of necessity

no longerAffirmative verbBefore main verb / after 'be'He no longer works here.
any longer / anymoreNegative verbAt the end of the sentenceHe doesn't work here anymore.

Rule: Use no longer with affirmative verbs (She no longer lives here). Use anymore or any longer with negative verbs (She doesn't live here anymore). Do NOT double-negative!

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Focus on natural sentence rhythm: emphasize the main content words when expressing No Longer, Any Longer, Anymore, while keeping grammatical function words unstressed.

Examples
  • I no longer drink coffee in the evening.
  • They don't speak to each other any longer.
⚠️ Common mistakes
❌He doesn't work here no longer.
tap to see the correct form
✅He doesn't work here anymore.

102 Past Simple vs Past Continuous

Level A2 Grammar Reference

Past Simple vs Past Continuous

Finished past actions vs past background activities in progress (Points 67 & 68)

🎯 Communicative Goal: Tell stories about past events, set background scenes, and describe interruptions using Past Continuous and Past Simple together.

👀 What do you notice?

Compare these two sentences:

  • "I cooked dinner yesterday." (Completed past action)
  • "I was cooking dinner when the phone rang." (Background activity in progress interrupted by a short event)

💡 Check your understanding (CCQs)

Score: 0 / 2
1. Which action started first in 'I was sleeping when the phone rang'?
Correct · Past Continuous sets the ongoing background scene; Past Simple interrupts it.
2. What structure is used for Past Continuous?
Correct · Form: Subject + was/were + verb-ing.

1. Past Simple vs Past Continuous Comparison

FeaturePast SimplePast Continuous
Core IdeaCompleted, finished action at a specific time in the pastAction in progress at a specific moment in the past
StructureVerb + -ed / irregular form (e.g. watched, went)was / were + verb-ing (e.g. was watching, were going)
ExamplesI watched a film yesterday.I was watching a film at 8 PM last night.

2. Combining Both: Background Action + Interruption (Point 68)

Rule: Use Past Continuous for the long background activity, and Past Simple for the short interrupting event.

  • ✅ I was sleeping (long) when the phone rang (short).
  • ✅ She was walking home when she saw an accident.
  • ✅ While I was studying, my friend called me.
⚠️ Common Mistakes
❌I was cook dinner yesterday.
tap to see the correct form
✅I cooked dinner yesterday. / I was cooking dinner yesterday at 7 PM.
(Finished past action without continuous time frame uses Past Simple)
❌When the phone rang, I slept.
tap to see the correct form
✅When the phone rang, I was sleeping.
(Background activity in progress requires Past Continuous)

🎯 Self-Evaluation Checklist

Quick Check Quiz

Score: 0 / 3

Short interrupting event takes Past Simple ('went').
2. 'At 9 o'clock last night, I ___ a book.'
Action in progress at a specific past time point → Past Continuous ('was reading').

Simple completed past action → Past Simple ('played').

SubjectAffirmativeNegativeQuestion

109 Present Perfect vs Past Simple

Present Perfect vs Past Simple

110 Present Simple vs Present Continuous

Part 0 · Quick A1 Review

Present Simple vs Present Continuous

Habits and permanent states vs actions happening right now

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can contrast daily habits and routines with actions happening at the moment of speaking.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. "He is cooking dinner." — Is he cooking right now in this current moment?
Correct · Present continuous describes actions happening right now at the time of speaking.
2. "They are staying at a hotel this week." — Is this a permanent home or a temporary situation?
Correct · Present continuous expresses temporary situations around the present time.
TenseUsageSignal WordsExample
Present SimpleHabits, routines, permanent factsalways, usually, every day, oftenI work in London every day.
Present ContinuousActions happening now, temporary trendsnow, at the moment, today, right nowI am working from home today.

Key Distinction: Use Present Simple for regular routines (I play tennis on Saturdays). Use Present Continuous for temporary actions happening right now or around now (I am playing tennis right now).

👀 Stative Verbs Warning

Verbs of thinking, feeling, and possessing (like know, want, like, understand, belong) are rarely used in continuous forms: I know the answer (NOT: I am knowing).

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

The third-person '-s' ending varies phonetically: /s/ after voiceless consonants (walks), /z/ after voiced sounds (runs), and /ɪz/ after sibilants (washes).

Examples
  • He usually drinks tea, but today he is drinking coffee.
  • What are you doing right now? I am studying grammar.
⚠️ Common mistakes
❌I am working in a bank every day.
tap to see the correct form
✅I work in a bank every day.
❌Look! It rains outside.
tap to see the correct form

SubjectObjectPossessive Adj (+ noun)Possessive Pronoun (alone)

114 Review of Verb Tenses

Part 3 · Future & Tense Review

Review of Verb Tenses

Side-by-side comparison of present, past, and future tenses

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can confidently select and alternate between all major A1–A2 verb tenses during continuous speech.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

Correct · This structure provides explicit grammatical function and clarity.
2. Form check: Does correct usage of Review of Verb Tenses require matching subject, verb, and modifier agreements?
Correct · Accurate form and agreement choices prevent misunderstandings.
TenseFormCore ConceptExample
Present Simpleverb / verb-sHabits & general truthsI work every day.
Present Continuousam/is/are + verb-ingActions right now / arrangementsI am working right now.
Past Simplepast form (-ed / irregular)Finished past actions at specific timeI worked yesterday.
Past Continuouswas/were + verb-ingAction in progress in the pastI was working at 4 PM.
Present Perfecthave/has + past participlePast connected to present / experienceI have worked here for years.
Future (Going to / Will)going to / will + verbIntentions vs instant decisionsI am going to work tomorrow. / I'll work late.

Mastery Checklist: Match the time adverbial to the correct tense: yesterday ➔ Past Simple; now ➔ Present Continuous; since 2020 ➔ Present Perfect; tomorrow ➔ Future.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

Focus on natural sentence rhythm: emphasize the main content words when expressing Review of Verb Tenses, while keeping grammatical function words unstressed.

Examples
  • Yesterday I went shopping, but today I am resting at home.

Correct · Accurate form and agreement choices prevent misunderstandings.
FormStructureExample
Affirmativesubject + should + verbYou should see a doctor.
Negativesubject + shouldn't + verbYou shouldn't drink cold water if you have a sore throat.
QuestionShould + subject + verb?Should I buy this jacket?

Rule: Should is followed by the base infinitive without 'to' (You should eat, NOT You should to eat). It expresses a good idea or advice, not a strict rule.

119 Used To: Past Habits & Past States

Part 1 · Talking About the Past

Used To: Past Habits & Past States

Things that were true in the past but are not true now

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can discuss long-term past habits, routines, and states that have since changed.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. Function check: What is the primary purpose of using Used To: Past Habits & Past States?
Correct · This structure provides explicit grammatical function and clarity.
2. Form check: Does correct usage of Used To: Past Habits & Past States require matching subject, verb, and modifier agreements?
Correct · Accurate form and agreement choices prevent misunderstandings.
FormStructureExample
Affirmativeused to + verbI used to live in Madrid.
Negativedidn't use to + verbShe didn't use to like spinach.
QuestionDid ... use to + verb?Did you use to play the piano?

Key Rule: used to + infinitive is ONLY for past habits and states that are NO LONGER true today. For negative forms and questions, drop the '-d': didn't use to, Did you use to...?

🔊 Pronunciation Note

Although written with a "d", used to is pronounced with an unvoiced /s/ sound and a weak schwa: /juːst tə/ (not /juːzd tuː/). In fast speech, the "d" blends completely into the "t".

Examples
  • I used to have long hair when I was a teenager.
  • We didn't use to travel much, but now we travel every year.
⚠️ Common mistakes
❌I use to play football every day when I was 10.
tap to see the correct form
✅I used to play football every day when I was 10.
❌I didn't used to like vegetables.
tap to see the correct form
✅I didn't use to like vegetables.

122 Will vs Going To

Part 3 · Future & Tense Review

Will vs Going To

Instant decisions vs pre-planned intentions

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can distinguish spontaneous decisions and offers from pre-planned intentions and evidence-based predictions.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. Function check: What is the primary purpose of using Will vs Going To?
Correct · This structure provides explicit grammatical function and clarity.
2. Form check: Does correct usage of Will vs Going To require matching subject, verb, and modifier agreements?
Correct · Accurate form and agreement choices prevent misunderstandings.
FormPrimary UseExample
Going ToPre-planned intentions, predictions with present evidenceI'm going to visit my grandmother this weekend. Look at those dark clouds, it's going to rain!
WillInstant decisions, promises, offers, predictions without evidenceThe phone is ringing. I'll answer it! I will help you carry those bags.

Rule: Did you decide BEFORE the moment of speaking? Use be going to. Are you deciding RIGHT NOW, offering help, or making a promise? Use will.

🗣️ Pronunciation Note

In spoken English, 'going to' reduces to 'gonna' /ˈɡənə/ in informal speech, while 'will' contracts smoothly to /l/ (she'll, they'll).

Examples
  • I am going to buy a new car next month (already decided).
  • I'm thirsty. I think I'll get a glass of water (spontaneous choice).
⚠️ Common mistakes
❌I decided yesterday: I will buy a laptop tomorrow.
tap to see the correct form
✅I decided yesterday: I am going to buy a laptop tomorrow.

Spontaneous instant decision at the moment of speaking takes 'will'.

Pre-planned intention with tickets bought takes 'are going to'.

B1 Intermediate Confusing Grammar Master Guide

A vs B (vs C) structural contrasts, logic maps, and usage guides for intermediate English learners

🎯 Master Goal: Express subtle differences in past experience, continuous duration, necessity, preference, and degree with intermediate fluency.

👀 What do you notice?

Compare these two intermediate sentences:

  • "I have painted the kitchen." (Result / finished action → kitchen is ready now)
  • "I have been painting the kitchen." (Duration / activity focus → my hands are covered in paint!)

💡 Check your understanding (CCQs)

Score: 0 / 2
1. Function check: If someone says "I've been waiting for two hours", are they emphasizing the duration of the activity or the completed result?
Correct · Present Perfect Continuous emphasizes the duration and continuous activity up to now.
2. Form check: What is the difference between 'so beautiful' and 'such a beautiful day'?
Correct · 'So' modifies adjectives alone (so warm); 'Such' modifies noun phrases (such a warm day).

🧠 Logic Map: Core B1 Grammar Contrasts

Structure AStructure B (vs C)Core Logic DifferenceKey Examples
Past Simple Present Perfect Simple Finished specific past time vs. Unspecified past time connected to now I lived in Rome in 2018. vs. I have lived in Rome for 3 years.
Present Perfect Simple Present Perfect Continuous Completed result / quantity vs. Duration of activity / ongoing action I have written 5 emails. vs. I have been writing emails all morning.
For Since / From Duration length vs. Specific starting point in time for 3 months | since March | from 9 AM to 5 PM
Didn't need to Needn't have Action was not necessary, so maybe not done vs. Action was done, but was unnecessary I didn't need to buy milk (so I didn't). vs. I needn't have bought milk (I bought it, but we had plenty).
So Such (a/an) So + adjective/adverb vs. Such + (a/an) + adjective + noun She is so smart. vs. She is such a smart person.
Another Other / The other / Others Another + singular countable vs. Other + plural vs. The other = remaining one another cup | other places | the other shoe | others agree
Wish + Past Simple Wish + Would Desire to change a present state vs. Desire for someone else to change annoying behavior I wish I was taller. vs. I wish you would stop tapping your pen!
⚠️ Common B1 Mistake Flips
❌I have seen him yesterday.
tap to see the correct form
✅I saw him yesterday.
('Yesterday' is a finished past time marker → Past Simple)
❌It was so good day!
tap to see the correct form
✅It was such a good day! / The day was so good!
('Such a + adjective + noun' vs 'So + adjective')
❌I have lived here since 5 years.
tap to see the correct form
✅I have lived here for 5 years. / ...since 2021.
('For' + duration; 'Since' + starting point)

Score: 0 / 3
1. 'It was ___ delicious meal that we ate everything.'
'Such a + adjective + singular noun' → 'such a delicious meal'.
2. 'I have been living here ___ 2020.'
2020 is a specific starting point in time → 'since'.

NO commas · 'that' allowed

EXTRA Information (Non-Defining)
USE commas · NO 'that'
My brother, who lives in London, is a doctor.

146 Modals of Deduction: Present (Must, Can't, Might/Could)

Part 4 · Modals & Nuance

Modals of Deduction: Present (Must, Can't, Might/Could)

can't be99% sure NO
might be30% possible
could be50% possible
should be80% expectation
must be99% sure YES

Making logical guesses about present situations

🎯 What you can communicate after this page: You can deduce information and express varying degrees of certainty about present facts.
🎯 Ready to test your skills? Reinforce this topic with interactive practice drills.

💡 Check your understanding

Score: 0 / 2
1. Function check: What is the primary purpose of using Modals of Deduction: Present (Must, Can't, Might/Could)?
Correct · This structure provides explicit grammatical function and clarity.
2. Form check: Does correct usage of Modals of Deduction: Present (Must, Can't, Might/Could) require matching subject, verb, and modifier agreements?
Correct · Accurate form and agreement choices prevent misunderstandings.
ModalDegree of CertaintyExample
must99% sure YES (logical conclusion)She has three sports cars. She must be rich.
might / may / could50% possible (maybe yes, maybe no)He's not answering. He might be busy.
can't99% sure NO (impossible)That can't be John. He's on vacation in Japan!

Rule: Modal + base infinitive. Use must when you are almost certain something is true. Use can't (NOT mustn't) when you are almost certain something is impossible.

🔊 Pronunciation

In deductions, "must" is usually pronounced in its weak form /məst/ or /məs/ in fast connected speech (He must be tired), but stressed to /mʌst/ when emphasizing certainty (He MUST be joking!).

Examples
  • Look at the long queue outside. It must be a great restaurant.
  • You've been working all day. You must be exhausted.
⚠️ Common mistakes
❌It mustn't be true! I don't believe it.
tap to see the correct form
✅It can't be true! I don't believe it.
